programs.good: Programs and Projects are grouped under one parent
programs.problem: The concept is correct, but the distinction between them is not explained strongly enough
programs.why: NGO/program users may not know which object to create
programs.rec: Keep one parent menu: Programs & Projects. Within it use Programs / Projects tabs

programs.problem: Slightly operational rather than strategic
programs.why: International Development organizations think in programs interventions and portfolios
programs.rec: Keep the name for now; use explanatory, microcopy: "Plan interventions, fund projects and track outcomes."

programs.good: Program has an outcome target and linked Project
programs.problem: Program is visually just anothers reporting container
programs.rec: s Treat Program as the strategic outcome layer

programs.good: Project has manager, budget, providers and beneficiaries
programs.problem: Project appears primarily as a budget container
programs.why: Project should represent an executable intervention
programs.rec: Show objective, geography, timeline, cohort, providers, budget and outcomes

programs.problem: Contradicts Create Program statement that programs do not hold budget
programs.why: This is a major data-model problem
programs.rec: Program budget envelope/Container project allocations.

programs.problem: Too little information to establish a serious development program
programs.why: Missing owner, end date, reporting cadence, geography and measurement framework
programs.rec: Keep Phase 1 lightweight but progressively disclose these fields

programs.problem: Good minimum viable flow
programs.why: Missing dates, objective, geography, capacity and parent program
programs.rec: Add optional fields progressively rather than turning creation into an enterprise form

programs.problem: It starts with object creation rather than the user's objective
programs.why: "Create program" may not be the user's actual intent
programs.rec: Entry should ask: "What are you trying to run?" Program / Project / Manage existing

programs.problem: No explanation of what happens next
programs.why: User may create an empty strategic object
programs.rec: Explain: "Set the outcome, then connect projects and cohorts."

programs.problem: Does not indicate whether project belongs to a program
programs.why: Users may create orphan projects unintentionally
programs.rec: Add optional Parent Program field with "No program / Org-wide project"

programs.good: Strong combination of budget and outcome information
programs.problem: Some visualizations are decorative rather than decision-oriented
programs.why: Executive users need decisions, not charts for their own sake
programs.rec: Every chart should answer a management question

programs.problem: "Active programmes" and program table count appear inconsistent i supplied screens
programs.rec: Ensure KPI, table and underlying records always reconcile

programs.problem: olio Does not distinguish unique beneficiaries from total enrolments
programs.why: One beneficiary can join multipl programs
programs.rec: Show Uniquee beneficiaries + Program enrolments separately

programs.problem: c It is unclear whether committed means allocated, reserved or spent
programs.rec: Define Allocated / Committed / Spent / Remaining. Does Committed mean "Actual Cost"? Is yes, default to "Actual Cost" terminology

programs.problem: Outcome denominator is not explained
programs.why: Finance and M&E users need methodology
programs.rec: Add tooltip: formula, verified-outcome definition and reporting period

programs.problem: Budget allocation gets more visual attention than outcomes
programs.rec: Pair allocation with outcome contribution

programs.problem: "Verified outcome" is not sufficiently defined
programs.rec: Add methodology / definition link

programs.problem: Some copy moves from data into a n without showing evidence
programs.rec: Use Observation Evidence Action structure

programs.problem: Sounds editorial and judgmental
programs.why: Institutional users need neutral operational language
programs.rec: Replace with: "Review allocation before next funding cycle."

programs.problem: Percentage alone lacks timeline context
programs.why: 76% spent may be healthy or dangerous depending on period
programs.rec: Show % spent + % time elapsed + forecast

programs.problem: Risk classification isn't consistently reflected across screens
programs.why: User may see "On track" while burn suggests risk
programs.rec: Use deterministic health logic

programs.problem: Current "Healthy / Watch / At risk" logic needs explicit rules
programs.rec: Document thresholds and surface them via tooltip

programs.problem: Too many KPIs compete equally
programs.rec: Prioritize 3 levels: Outcome / Delivery / Finance

programs.problem: is "Active" doesn't mean healthy
programs.rec: Separate Lifecycle status from Health status

programs.problem: Screen simultaneously says "On pace" while only 630k remains and project ends in 11 days
programs.rec: Change to At risk / Near budget limit

programs.problem: The chart is too dominant relative to intervention controls
programs.why: User sees problem but has limited next action
programs.rec: Place Adjust budget / Cap enrolment / Review spend directly beside warning

programs.good: "Exhausts 2 Oct at this rate" is powerful
programs.problem: Forecast methodology isn't explained
programs.rec: Add "Based on current daily spend" and forecast confidence/data period

programs.problem: It currently describes a funnel but does not make each stage actionable
programs.why: 11 never-booked beneficiaries are a retention opportunity
programs.rec: Make every stage clickable

programs.problem: Consent is treated as a number rather than workflow state
programs.rec: Link pending consent to a specific beneficiary action queue

programs.problem: Activation isn't clearly defined
programs.rec: Define activation precisely

programs.problem: "Still active" needs a formal definition
programs.rec: Define 30-day/period-ba sed activity

programs.good: Excellent decision to map providers at Project level
programs.problem: Correctly supports granular tracking
programs.rec: Keep Project-level and Cohort-level provider assignment

programs.problem: Too shallow
programs.why: Program managers need utilization, capacity and service-delivery quality
programs.rec: Add sessions, active beneficiaries, spend, availability and aggregate performance

programs.problem: It looks very similar to a Project dashboard
programs.rec: Program page should emphasize target portfolio outcomes allocation

programs.problem: No baseline / current / target explanation
programs.rec: Show Baseline Current Target

programs.problem: Measurement period isn't strongly connected to baseline
programs.rec: Display baseline date, current value and target date

programs.problem: Project health is visible only as utilization
programs.rec: Add project contribution to program target

programs.problem: Could be duplicate-counted
programs.rec: Clearly distinguish unique beneficiaries vs total program enrollments

programs.problem: Spend concentration warning is useful
programs.rec: Keep and add outcome contribution beside spend

programs.problem: Engagement only
programs.why: Cohorts should become operational M&E units
programs.rec: Add cohort target, enrollment, activation, utilization, outcomes and spend

programs.problem: Existing project selection may be too early
programs.rec: Allow create first; link Projects during setup or later

programs.problem: Privacy is buried in creation form
programs.why: Privacy is foundational in PO architecture
programs.rec: Keep, but add concise explanation and link to policy

programs.problem: Need stronger consistency with PO privacy model
programs.rec: Make visibility rules explicit per Program/Project

programs.problem: Not sufficiently integrated
programs.why: Programs are where ROI should be generated
programs.rec: Add persistent View Impact Report action

programs.problem: Finance is treated as a number, not workflow
programs.why: Programs should connect allocation to spending
programs.rec: Add "Open budget" and allocation history

programs.problem: No commercial growth loop visible
programs.why: Platform revenue is tied to funded activity
programs.rec: Contextually surface expansion opportunities

programs.problem: Missed opportunity
programs.why: Growing organizations will need more capacity/reporting
programs.rec: Use threshold-based, non-intrusive prompts

programs.problem: Missed opportunity. Program data could drive adjacent EH services
programs.rec: Suggest relevant providers, reporting, additional Projects or enterprise billing where contextually relevant

programs.problem: Good conversion mechanism
programs.rec: Show program setup dependencies: verification funding project beneficiaries providers

programs.problem: Placeholder mixes beneficiaries, projects and invoices
programs.rec: Use global search but add object-type filters

programs.problem: Large NGOs will quickly outgrow this
programs.rec: Filter by program, project, geography, status, manager, cohort, provider, funding source

programs.problem: Several sample screens contain different project/program names and amounts
programs.why: Prototype inconsistency can become backend inconsistency
programs.rec: Establish one canonical demo dataset

programs.problem: Charts rely heavily on color
programs.rec: Use labels, patterns, icons and text status in addition to color

programs.problem: Currently more like an analytics dashboard than a program-management operating system
programs.why: It does not yet fully support the PO lifecycle
programs.rec: Evolve into Program → Project → Cohort → Delivery → Finance → Outcomes operating model

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Add a Finance landing page before Wallet & Funding. Show available funds, committed funds, allocated budgets, actual spend, pending settlements, invoices due and alerts. Add a reporting-period selector and links to detailed views.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Finance users immediately understand the organisation's financial positio and know what requires attention.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Better finance usability and institutional confidence. n

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Create separate cards for Available, Allocated, Committed, Reserved, Spent and Pending Settlement. Add short definitions or tooltips explaining each balance.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users can distinguish spendable money from money already assigned, reserved or awaiting settlement.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Fewer financial misunderstandings and support requests.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Define and document the relationship between wallet balance, project budgets, allowances, seats, escrow, provider payables and pending transactions. Show how each figure is calculated.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: All displayed totals reconcile to agreed business rules and the relevant financial records. No overlapping figures are presented as independent balances.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Financial trust and reliable decision-making.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Allow users to click a balance card and see the underlying credits, debits, holds, allocations and other components that explain the figure.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users can understand why a balance has its current value without contacting support.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Faster financial investigation.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Show funds held in escrow, the related engagement or transaction, amount reserved, release conditions, expected release date where known, and amount released.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users can distinguish available wallet funds from funds held pending an event or condition.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Transparent financial operations and stronger provider trust.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Show funds awaiting settlement separately from completed wallet credits, provider payouts and reconciled transactions. Include the transaction reference, amount, date and status.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users understand why a payment or payout has not yet become available or completed.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Better cash-position visibility and reconciliation.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Standardise statuses such as Pending, Processing, Completed, Failed, Reversed, Refunded, Disputed and Reconciliation Required. Confirm which statuses apply to each transaction type.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Status labels are consistent across wallet, transactions, invoices, escrow, refunds and payouts.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Less confusion and fewer incorrect actions.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Show actor, action, timestamp, affected record, reason, reference and before/after values for material changes. Include budget edits, funding rules, approvals and financial adjustments.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users with the relevant permission can trace who did what, when and why.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Enterprise governance and auditability.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Create approval journeys for actions that require authorisation, such as high-value funding, budget increases, auto-reload changes, billing-mode changes, refunds and payouts. Configure thresholds only after the business rules are confirmed.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: The requester can track the request; authorised approvers can approve or reject it; the final statu is visible and auditable.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Segregation of duties and institutional readiness. s

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Create a central list of actions awaiting approval. Show request type, amount, requester, project/programme, submission date, urgency and status. Include detail, approve, reject and request-changes actions as permitted.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Approvers can identify and process outstanding decisions without searching across multiple modules.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Faster workflows and fewer operational delays.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Organise the page around Available Funds, Funding Sources, Add Funds, Auto-Reload, Escrow and Funding History. Avoid mixing balance information with unrelated settings.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Finance users can find the correct funding task quickly and understand the current state of their funds.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Finance becomes a practical treasury-control workspace.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Create a clear sequence: enter amount select funding source review fees and limits view expected balance impact complete required authorisation confirm. Show the transaction reference and next steps after submission.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users understand exactly what they are authorising before initiating payment.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Improved funding conversion and fewer mistakes.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Design a funding-source list for payment methods supported by the confirmed Phase 1 payment integration. Allow users to add, view, select, remove or update sources where supported. Distinguish verified and unverified sources.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users can identify the funding source being used and manage it within their permissions.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Enterprise flexibility and a smoother funding journey.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Where supported by the business model, capture funding attribution such as Grant, Donor, Corporate, Government or Internal Funds. Do not treat an attribution label as proof that the source has been verified.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Funds can be associated with the correct source for reporting and budget governance.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Better funder reporting and programme accountability.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Separate the payment provider's reported status from ElevatedHere's interpretation and next-step guidance. Design distinct states for decline, timeout, pending confirmation and confirmed failure.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users are not told a payment failed if its final outcome is still unknown.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Reduced confusion and duplicate payments.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: For each failed or unresolved payment, provide the appropriate next action: check status, retry safely, change method, follow bank-transfer instructions where supported, or contact support. Preserve the transaction reference.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users know how to recover from a payment problem without restarting the entire journey or creating duplicate attempts.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Lower payment abandonment and fewer support escalations.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: On successful funding, show the confirmed amount, transaction reference, payment method, updated balance and receipt action. Add Allocate Funds and View Transaction shortcuts.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: The user can verify the result and move directly to the next relevant task.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Converts successful funding into programme activation.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Add trigger threshold, reload amount, selected source, frequency/limit rules where supported, notification preferences, authorisation and rule status. Provide Edit, Pause and Disable actions.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Users understand when a charge will occur and can control or stop automatic funding.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Funding continuity with appropriate financial safeguards.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Design alerts for low balance, failed funding, pending payment, high burn rate, budget threshold, overdue invoice and relevant escrow events. Link each alert to the record or action that resolves it.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Alerts are specific, actionable and dismissible where appropriate; users are not forced to hunt for the issue.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Reduced operational failures and interruptions.

Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.work: Create a searchable list of successful, pending and failed funding attempts, with date, amount, source, status and reference.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.accept: Finance can trace funding activity from initiation through the final confirmed status.
Table 1 — Finance Overview, Funding and.impact: Better reconciliation and customer support.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Show Budget Cap, Committed, Spent, Remaining/Available and Forecast where supported. Include the project/programme name, period and budget status.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can distinguish approved allocation, actual consumption and outstanding commitments.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Better programme and budget management.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Introduce Healthy, Watch, At Risk and Exhausted states. Define thresholds with the product owner and finance lead. Consider utilisation, remaining funds and burn rate rather than relying on one percentage alone.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Budget health communicates a meaningful financial condition, not just a decorative progress bar.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Earlier intervention and better expenditure control.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Design Draft Pending Approval Active Near Limit Exhausted Closed. Add Rejected or Cancelled where the confirmed workflow requires them.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Each budget has a clear status and users can understand which actions are available at each stage.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Consistent budget lifecycle and fewer operational errors.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Add budget name, purpose, funding source, programme/project, amount, budget period, owner, eligible spending categories or services where applicable, and approval requirements. Show the wallet balance and remaining unallocated funds before submission.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can create a budget with sufficient context and understand the impact on available funds before confirming.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Controlled allocation and reduced misallocation.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Allow authorised users to associate a pool with approved programmes, projects, regions, services or beneficiary cohorts where the product rules support restrictions. Show restrictions clearly on the budget detail page.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can understand where funds may and may not be used. Restricted funds cannot be presented as unrestricted spending capacity.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Donor/grant governance and programme accountability.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Add budget cap, spent, committed, available, forecast where supported, members/beneficiaries, related transactions, linked allowances, allocation history and approval history.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Finance users can investigate the budget and its financial activity from one page.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Better financial control and faster investigations.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Design Request More Budget enter amount provide reason identify funding source or proposed reallocation submit approver decision status update.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Requests can be tracked from submission to final decision. Requested funds do not appear as available before approval and allocation.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Enterprise controls and predictable programme spending.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Add requested amount, justification, urgency, required date, affected programme/project, source of additional funding where known and relevant supporting information.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Approvers have enough information to decide without repeatedly requesting missing details.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Faster budget decisions and less administrative friction.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Create distinct actions for Request Additional Funds, Reallocate Existing Funds and Change Approved Budget Cap. Explain the effect of each action before submission.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users understand whether they are requesting new money, moving existing funds or changing an authorised limit.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Prevents misleading balances and uncontrolled expenditure.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Show previous and new budget values, actor, reason, approval, date and related funding source for each change.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can trace the history of budget changes without relying on manual records.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Audit readiness and transparent governance.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Design notifications for approaching limits, exhaustion, unusual burn rate, pending budget approval and unused allocations near their end date where dates exist.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: The right person receives a relevant alert with a direct route to the affected budget.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Reduced service interruption and under-utilised funding.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Show average weekly or monthly expenditure over a clearly stated period. Explain the calculation and exclude or separately identify commitments where appropriate.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users understand the rate at which a programme consumes funds and can inspect the underlying data.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Better financial planning.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Show an estimated depletion date or future spend projection only where sufficient, reliable historical and commitment data exists. State the assumptions and period used.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Forecasts are clearly labelled as estimates and can be traced to their underlying calculation.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Improved treasury planning without overstating certainty.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Display estimated months or weeks of funding remaining when the calculation is meaningful. Show the period and burn-rate assumptions used.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: The user can understand how long funds may last at the current rate and see why the estimate may change.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Earlier funding and programme-c ontinuity planning.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Where required by the customer model, support attribution to department, programme, grant, region or other approved cost centre.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Expenditure can be grouped by an agreed organisational structure without relying on free-text labels alone.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Enterprise accounting and institutional adoption.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Create a drill-down from Project Budget Spend Provider/Service Provider Engagement or service reference, subject to access permissions.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can trace programme expenditure to its relevant financial and operational records without exposing private service content.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Programme management and financial accountability.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Where permitted, show beneficiary reference, allowance, consumed amount, remaining allowance and linked transactions. Use privacy-safe identifiers where possible.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Finance can understand sponsorship utilisation without access to private clinical notes, case evidence or session content.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: B2B2C financial transparency and beneficiary privacy.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Add allowance scope, eligible members, effective date, frequency, expiry, rollover rules, service restrictions, exhaustion behaviour and exception rules.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can understand how allowance policies work and who will be affected by a change.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Prevents uncontrolled spending and inconsistent benefits.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Design individual or cohort exceptions with reason, requested change, effective date, authorisation, status and history. Include bulk-change review.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Exceptions are visible, controlled and auditable rather than silently overriding the default policy.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Better expenditure control at scale.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Show the number of eligible, assigned, active and excluded members or beneficiaries where these concepts are supported. Explain how allocations relate to the programme budget.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: Users can understand the population covered and the effect of allocating funds or allowances.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Better programme planning and utilisation.

Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.work: Design the close-budget action with remaining balance, outstanding commitments, pending payments and unresolved exceptions.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.accept: A budget cannot appear cleanly closed while unresolved financial items are hidden from the user.
Table 2 — Budget Pools, Programme Fundin.impact: Stronger financial governance and accurate reporting.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Separate Invoices from Subscriptions & Seats conceptually, even if they remain under one Finance navigation group. Give each area its own list, filters and primary actions.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users understand the difference between an amount owed and a subscription or seat entitlement.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Show invoice number, billing period, issue date, due date, total, amount paid, outstanding amount, currency and status. Add filters for paid, unpaid, overdue, disputed and draft where applicable.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Finance users can identify outstanding liabilities or receivables and find the relevant invoice quickly.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Include invoice line items, programme/project, funding source, billing period, applicable fees/taxes, total, amount paid, balance due, payment status and related transaction references.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: A downloadable invoice can be traced to the relevant charges and payment records.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Provide View, Download, Pay where supported, Dispute, Share and View Related Transactions. Display actions only when valid for the invoice status and user's permissions.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can take the appropriate next step without ambiguity or unavailable actions.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.impact: Complete invoice lifecycle and fewer billing queries.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Design Draft, Issued, Pending Payment, Partially Paid where supported, Paid, Overdue, Disputed, Cancelled and Credited/Adjusted states as appropriate.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Statuses reflect the actual invoice lifecycle and do not imply payment when only an invoice has been issued.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Display due dates, approved payment terms and the relevant billing contact or escalation route where available. Do not imply that credit terms are available to every organisation.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Organisations understand when payment is due and what terms apply to their account.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.task: Add Credit Note / Invoice Adjustment Flow
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: If in Phase 1, design the adjustment request, reason, affected invoice, amount, approval and relationship to the original invoice.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Adjustments are linked to the original invoice and traceable through their lifecycle.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Show purchased, assigned, active, unused, available and renewal seats where these are distinct in the product model. Include plan, period, cost and linked programme/project.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can understand the number of seats purchased, assigned and available, and what they are paying for.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Design selection of eligible members/cohorts, seat assignment, confirmation, assignment success and removal/reassignment states. Explain billing consequences where applicable.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users understand who receives a seat and whether changing an assignment affects billing o access.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.impact: Easier programme activation and administration. r

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Where subscriptions are in Phase 1, show active plan, billing period, renewal date, status, upgrade/downgrade options and cancellation consequences.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can manage their plan with clear pricing and timing information.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Where postpaid invoicing, custom billing or a large programme is unavailable for self-service, add Talk to ElevatedHere about enterprise billing or a suitabl request/demo action.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users have a clear path forward instead of encountering a dead end e when their requirements exceed self-service functionality.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Add transaction reference, date/time, transaction type, payer/source, recipient/destination where relevant, project/programme, provider/beneficiary reference, gross amount, fees, net amount and status.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Finance users can filter, searc and identify transactions without depending on informal labels alone.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.impact: Better financial h investigation and reporting.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Show unique reference, event timeline, payer, recipient, source, destination, gross, fee breakdown, net amount, currency, funding source, status, related invoice, budget and original transaction where relevant.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Finance can investigate the transaction without losing the context of the transaction list.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Design a dedicated ledger view with posting date, journal reference, account, debit, credit, currency, source transaction and audit history, subject to confirmation of the accounting architecture.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can distinguish operational transaction history from formal accounting postings.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: ElevatedHere is intended to own the accounting system of record, design the account list, account codes, account type, status and account-detail view.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: The interface reflects the agreed accounting architecture rather than suggesting that a transaction list is a complete general ledger.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Design a workspace for matching payment gateway transactions wallet ledger escrow movements provider payouts. Include statement/settlement batch, matched/unmatched records, discrepancy amount, owner and resolution status.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Finance can identify mismatches, investigate them and track their resolution.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Create detail states for missing transactions, duplicate references, amount mismatches, timing differences and unresolved settlement items, where these can occur in the actual integration.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Exceptions have a clear explanation, responsible owner and next action.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Design refund/reversal request, original transaction link, reason, amount, affected budget, approval, processing status, failure handling and audit trail. Include disputed/chargeback states to the payment integration.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Every adjustment can be traced to its original event and its final outcome.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.impact: Safe financial recovery and complete transaction lifecycle.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Show provider, engagement/service reference, gross amount, platform fee, payment fees where applicable, net payable, escrow status, payout status, payment date and reference.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Finance can understand how an engagement's amount relates to the provider's expected and completed payout.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.impact: Provider trust and transparent financial operations.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Display service amount, platform commission, payment processing fee, applicable taxes and other charges separately wherever relevant..
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can understand how the total amount is calculated and how the amount payable differs from platform revenue.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: multi-currency is in scope, so display transaction currency, settlement currency, reporting currency, exchange rate, rate date/time, converted amount and applicable FX fees.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: The interface never silently treats values in different currencies as directly comparable.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Provide CSV/PDF exports for transactions, budgets, invoices and reconciliation records, with filters by date, project, provider, beneficiary reference where permitted, funding source and currency.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can export records for finance review and reporting without manually rebuilding the data in spreadsheets.

Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.work: Where required, show export availability by role and record export activity for sensitive financial reports. Clearly indicate applied filters and reporting period.
Table 3 — Invoices, Seats, Transactions.accept: Users can tell what data is being exported and whether their role permits the action.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Add a report catalogue covering financial transactions, budget performance, invoice status, programme spend, provider payments and funding utilisation.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Finance users can find the appropriate report without navigating through individual operational screens.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Better reporting efficiency and enterprise adoption.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Add a View Programme Performance or View Impact of This Spend action from relevant budget, project and transaction views. Carry the relevant project/programme and reporting period into the destination report.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Users can move from a financial record to its related utilisation and outcome information without restarting their search.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Connects financial operations to measurable programme value.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: On a programme or impact report, add View Investment Behind This Outcome. Link to the associated project, budget and expenditure records subject to the user's permissions.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Users can trace reported programme results to the relevant financial investment.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Greater funder confidence and improved renewal discussions.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Create views of expenditure by programme, project, provider, service and reporting period. Include budget versus actual spend and relevant utilisation measures.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Finance users can see where money is going and compare expenditure with service delivery.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Better resource allocation and programme management.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Define the calculation as eligible programme expenditure divided by an agreed beneficiary denominator. Show the selected period, population, inclusions and exclusions.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Users understand what the metric means and which beneficiaries and costs were included.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Distinguish total beneficiarie covered from beneficiaries who actively used a service during the reporting period. Document the active-use definition.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: s Cost comparisons do not confuse assigned or eligible members with actual service users.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Better utilisation and funding-efficie ncy analysis.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Connect relevant expenditure with completed sessions or delivered services. Define how cancelled, refunded, unpaid and externally paid services are treated.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: The denominator and included expenditure are explicit, and users can drill down to supporting records.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Better service economics and procurement decisions.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: If outcome data and methodology are available, connect verified programme outcomes with relevant expenditure. Document the outcome definition, measurement period and cost attribution.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: The metric is only displayed when sufficient valid data exists; users can inspect the methodology and limitations.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: More credible donor and programme evaluation.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Compare budget utilisation with relevant programme engagement, such as eligible beneficiaries, active beneficiaries and completed services. Avoid implying that utilisation alone proves effectiveness.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Finance users can see the relationship between expenditure and programme activity without confusing activity with impact.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Design an ROI view only after the product owner defines what constitutes a return, how it is valued and which costs and outcomes are included. Display the calculation and assumptions.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: ROI is not presented as a generic score or calculated from spend and activity alone.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Credible programme evaluation and renewal support.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Where a validated methodology exists, show the relationship between investment, reach, utilisation and measured outcomes. Explain the methodology and any monetised assumptions.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: The report distinguishes financial expenditure, service reach, measured outcomes and estimated social value.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Design an exportable programme report combining approved financial information, budget performance, beneficiary reach, utilisation and permitted outcome metrics. Include reporting period and funding-source attribution.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: The report can be understood outside ElevatedHere and contains clear definitions, totals and relevant supporting details.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: If multi-country or regional reporting is supported, allow expenditure and budgets to be grouped by country, region, programme and project. Show currency context for each view.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Users can understand geographic spending without mixing currencies or losing the underlying project attribution.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: If required by target organisations, support approved financial-year and reporting-period views, including quarter-based reporting such as FY/Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4. Confirm how these periods are configured.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Users can filter and compare expenditure against the organisation's agreed reporting calendar.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Where required, capture and display purchase order number, grant code, contract reference and other agreed institutional identifiers on relevant budgets, invoices and transactions.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Finance teams can search and reconcile records against their internal procurement or grant-management references.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Where sufficient comparable data exists, allow users to compare current programme expenditure and utilisation with previous periods. Clearly identify differences i scope, population and methodology.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Comparisons use consistent definitions or explain wheren definitions differ.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Consolidate low balance, high burn, approaching budget limits, overdue invoices, unused allocations and relevant pending approvals into an actionable alert view.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Each alert explains the issue, its affected record and the available next action.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.impact: Reduced funding interruptions and better oversight.

Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.task: Add Report Definitions and Data Freshness
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.work: Show report date range, last updated time, calculation definitions and any material data limitations. Distinguish provisional information from confirmed financial records where necessary.
Table 4 — Financial Reports, Programme E.accept: Users understand what the report represents and whether all relevant transactions have been processed.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Let prospective organisations understand the platform and explore permitted areas before completing every administrative requirement. Add a guided checklist for organisation verification, authorised signatory, billing/funding setup and activation.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users can see what remains to be completed and why each requirement matters. Funding and activation remain gated where verification is mandatory.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Less onboarding abandonment without weakening controls.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Show Not Started, In Progress, Action Required, Approved or Rejected where those states match the actual verification workflow. Provide the required next step and a route to resolve problems.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users understand the verification status and can continue from where they stopped.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Begin with the organisation's objective--such as funding a wellness programme, sponsoring beneficiaries, managing service access or reporting programme expenditure--before exposing complex module choices.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users can identify a relevant starting poin without understanding ElevatedHere's internal role or module structure.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Highert activation and less early-stage confusion.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Allow users to explore permitted features and prepare draft configurations before completing steps that are only required for funding or go-live. Save progress and explain blocked actions.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users can experience value early, while mandatory compliance and financial gates remain intact.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: After organisation setup or funding, guide the user to the next meaningful action: create a programme/project, allocate funds, configure allowances or enrol eligible beneficiaries.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users know how to move from setup to actual programme activation.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Faster time to value and better retention.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: For organisations needing custom billing, large-scale deployment, procurement support or unavailable self-service features, add a clear Talk to ElevatedHere or Request a Consultation action.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users have a viable next step when their needs exceed the available self-service workflow.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Enterprise lead generation and assisted conversion.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Compare prepaid wallet, postpaid invoicing and per-seat subscription using payment timing, fees, eligibility, limits, operational requirements and the appropriate next step. Confirm which options are actually available in Phase 1.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users understand the consequences of choosing a billing model. Unavailable options are clearly labelled rather than presented as functional.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Better commercial conversion and fewer abandoned selections.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Design in-product notification patterns for lo balances, pending approvals, budget exhaustion, invoice due dates and failed payments. Define which roles receive each notification with the product owner.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Alerts reach relevant w users and provide a direct link to the action or record that needs attention.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Fewer missed actions and programme interruptions.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Create role-appropriate views for Owner, Admin/Manager, Project Manager, Finance/Billing and Analyst/Viewer, using the permissions defined in the PO Concept Note.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users see the functions relevant to their role without being given unauthorised financial access.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Distinguish View, Create, Edit, Submit for Approval, Approve, Export and Administer permissions. Design hidden/disabled actions and clear permission-denied states.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: The interface communicates why an action is unavailable and what authorised route exists, without exposing protected information.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Reduced risk and fewer operational errors.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Keep clinical notes, session content, dispute/case evidence and other private service information out of PO finance views. Define which named operational information is permitted fo each role and consent context.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Finance reporting provides the necessary financial information without becoming a route to private beneficiary content. r

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Where outcome reporting is permitted, show appropriately aggregated data and apply the approved minimum cohort/privacy rules. Avoid presenting small groups in ways that expose individual identities.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Reports provide useful programme information without revealing sensitive individual data.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: If an organisation pays a provider outside ElevatedHere, distinguish Paid Through ElevatedHere from Recorded Externally. Provide fields for an external reference and evidence where required.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Reports do not imply that externally recorded payments were processed or reconciled by ElevatedHere.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Accurate expenditure reporting and provider transparency.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Design meaningful first-use states for no funding sources, no budgets, no transactions, no invoices, no reports and no pending approvals. Provide one relevant next action per state.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: New organisations know how to begin instead of encountering blank tables or unexplained zero values.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Design loading, validation, session expiry, gateway timeout, permission denial, export failure and recoverable system-error states for core finance tasks. Preserve entered information when safe.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Users understand what happened and how to recover without losing work unnecessarily.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Better UX reliability and fewer support requests.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Check typography, contrast, keyboard navigation, focus states, error messaging, table responsiveness and status indicators. Ensure status i not communicated through colour alone.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Core financial tasks remain understandable and usable across supported screens sizes and interaction methods.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Broader usability and reduced training burden.

Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.work: Create reusable components for amount/currency fields, status badges, tables, alerts, confirmation dialogs, approval states, filters, date ranges and transaction references.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.accept: Finance screens use consistent labels, spacing, interaction patterns and status meanings.
Table 5 — Enterprise Readiness, Security.impact: Faster design and development with less inconsistency.

Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.work: Document all Finance pages, navigation items, detail views, drawers, modals and links to related PO modules.
Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.accept: No required Finance task is missing from the screen inventory.

Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.work: Map funding, allocation, allowance setup, invoice review, transaction investigation, approval, reconciliation and reporting from start to completion.
Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.accept: Each critical task has a clear starting point, success state and recovery route.

Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.work: For each core screen, list its default, empty, loading, success, pending, error, restricted-access and completed states as applicable.
Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.accept: No critical action is designed only for the happy path.

Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.work: Review all displayed sample balances, budget calculations, fees, transaction statuses and report figures with the relevant finance/engineering stakeholders.
Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.accept: Sample data follows the documented rules and balances reconcile across connected screens.

Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.work: Check every finance screen and export for role-based access, beneficiary-data exposure and approval restrictions.
Table 6 — Final Phase 1 Design Handoff a.accept: Users cannot access information or actions outside the agreed permission model.
